tips.title: y goes before its own verb
tips.body: *J'y vais.* *J'y suis allé* — before the **auxiliary**. *Je vais y aller* — before the **infinitive**, because it is *aller* that goes to the place, not *vais*. One rule, three cases.

tips.title: chez takes a person
tips.body: *Chez moi*, *chez Marie*, *chez le médecin*. Never *chez la maison* — a house is not somebody. And *chez* does not change for movement: *je vais chez moi*, *je suis chez moi*.

tips.title: chambre is a bedroom
tips.body: *Ma maison a six chambres* claims six **bedrooms**. Any room is **une pièce**, so *six pièces* is almost certainly what you meant. The two sentences describe different houses.

tips.title: Les toilettes are plural
tips.body: *Les toilettes **sont** au rez-de-chaussée*, with *sont*, not *est*. French treats it as plural where English does not, and the verb has to follow.

tips.title: Reality, opinion, dream, reason
tips.body: Four sentences in that order give you two tenses, two opinions and a link word. A list of eight rooms gives one tense and no opinions — and scores lower for being longer.

tips.title: Y marks the spot
tips.body: *Y* is the X on the map: here it stands for a place phrase with *à*, *dans*, *en* or *chez*, and sits just before the verb that goes there (after it, with a hyphen, in a positive command: *vas-y*). *J'**y** vais*, *j'**y** suis allé*, *je vais **y** aller*.

why.matters: The ideal home is a dream, and dreams are the conditional: *ma maison idéale serait au bord de la mer, il y aurait une piscine*. The topic exists for that, and for three small words the real home needs first: the floors, *le rez-de-chaussée* counted the British way; *chez*, which takes a person and never a place; and *y*, which means *there* and goes in front of the verb it belongs to, *j'y vais, je vais y aller*. Reality, opinion, dream, reason is the shape of the answer, and it carries two tenses by itself.

examples.title: Le rez-de-chaussée
examples.body: The French ground floor is *le rez-de-chaussée*, and the floor above it is *le premier étage*, exactly as in Britain and unlike America, so a French flat *au deuxième étage* is two flights up. *Au* goes with a floor, *ma chambre est au premier étage*, and *une chambre* is a bedroom while *une pièce* is any room, a distinction a text about a house relies on. Say what is where and the description has a plan.

visual.alt: A table of French words for floors and rooms with their English meanings, including the ground floor counted the British way and the plural toilettes

examples.title: Chez moi
examples.body: *Chez* means *at the home of* and takes a person, never a place: *chez moi, chez Marie, chez le médecin*, and it does not change for movement, *je vais chez moi* and *je suis chez moi* alike. For a place the preposition is *à, dans* or *en*: *à la maison, dans la cuisine, en ville*. English *at* covers both, which is why *chez la maison* is the error to watch for.

visual.alt: A table showing chez with a person, moi and le médecin, against à, dans and en with places

examples.title: J'y vais: y before its verb
examples.body: *Y* means *there* and replaces a whole place phrase: *tu vas à la piscine ? oui, j'y vais*. It goes immediately before the verb it belongs to, which settles the hard cases: before the auxiliary in the perfect, *j'y suis allé*, and before the infinitive after a modal, *je vais y aller*, because it is *aller* that goes there, not *vais*. *Je* elides before it, *j'y*, and the imperative gets its *s* back for the sound, *vas-y*.

steps.title: Où j'habite
steps.body:
Start with what is true, because the ideal home is only interesting next to the real one.

- **J'habite dans une maison / dans un appartement.** — I live in a house / a flat.
- **J'habite en ville / à la campagne / en banlieue / au bord de la mer.** — in town / in the country / in the suburbs / by the sea.
- **Ma maison est grande / petite / moderne / ancienne.**

**The floors** are numbered as they are in Britain — the ground floor is not counted as the first:

| French | English |
|---|---|
| *le rez-de-chaussée* | the ground floor |
| *le premier étage* | the first floor |
| *le deuxième étage* | the second floor |

And **au** goes with a floor: *ma chambre est **au** premier étage*, *la cuisine est **au** rez-de-chaussée*.

**Habiter is regular.** *J'habite, tu habites, il habite, nous habitons, vous habitez, ils habitent* — an ordinary *-er* verb, and one you will use in every answer in this topic. Note *j'habite* with an apostrophe: the **h** is silent.

steps.title: Les pièces de la maison
steps.body:
The rooms, with their genders — and the gender matters, because everything you say about a room has to agree with it.

- **la cuisine** — the kitchen
- **le salon** — the living room
- **la salle à manger** — the dining room
- **la salle de bains** — the bathroom
- **la chambre** — the bedroom
- **le bureau** — the study, or the office
- **les toilettes** (f, plural) — the toilet
- **l'entrée** (f) — the hall
- **le sous-sol** — the basement
- **le grenier** — the attic

**Two that catch people out:**

- **Une chambre** is a **bedroom**, not any room. A room in general is *une pièce*. *Ma maison a six pièces* — my house has six rooms.
- **Les toilettes** is **plural** in French, and feminine: *les toilettes sont au rez-de-chaussée*, with *sont*, not *est*.

**Saying where a room is** uses the prepositions you already have: *à côté de* (next to), *en face de* (opposite), *au-dessus de* (above), *au-dessous de* (below), *entre… et…* (between… and…).

*Ma chambre est **à côté de la** salle de bains, **au-dessus du** salon.*

steps.title: Chez
steps.body:
**Chez** is one of the most useful words in French and it has **no single English word**. It means *at the home of*, or *at the place of*.

- **chez moi** — at my house, at my place
- **chez toi** — at your house
- **chez nous** — at our house
- **chez mes grands-parents** — at my grandparents'
- **chez Marie** — at Marie's

English needs an apostrophe and a guessed noun — *at Marie's* (house? shop? office?). French just says **chez Marie**.

**It works for businesses too**, because a shop is the place of the person who runs it:

- **chez le médecin** — at the doctor's
- **chez le coiffeur** — at the hairdresser's
- **chez le dentiste** — at the dentist's

**And it covers going as well as being**, with no change: *je vais **chez moi*** — I'm going home. *Je suis **chez moi*** — I'm at home. The preposition does not change for movement, which is unusual and worth noticing.

**Chez takes a person, never a place.** *Chez la maison* is wrong — a house is not somebody. For a place you use *à*, *dans* or *en*: *à la maison*, *dans la cuisine*, *en ville*.

steps.title: Le pronom y
steps.body:
**Y** means **there**. It replaces a whole phrase naming a place — *à Paris*, *dans ma chambre*, *chez moi*, *en France* — so you do not have to say the place twice. On the Pearson specification *y* is Higher tier grammar.

- *Tu vas **à Paris** ?* — *Oui, **j'y** vais.* — Yes, I'm going **there**.
- *Tu habites **dans cette maison** ?* — *Oui, **j'y** habite depuis cinq ans.*

**Where it goes: immediately before the verb it belongs to.** That one rule covers every case except the positive imperative, where *y* follows the verb with a hyphen (see below).

- Simple tense — before the verb: **j'y vais**, **nous y habitons**
- Perfect tense — before the **auxiliary**, not the participle: **j'y suis allé**
- With an infinitive — the place belongs to the infinitive, so **y** goes in front of **that**: **je vais y aller**, **on peut y aller à pied**

$$\textbf{je} \to \textbf{j'} \; \text{before y}$$

*Y* begins with a vowel sound, so *je* elides: **j'y vais**, never *je y vais*.

**In the imperative there is a small surprise.** The *tu* imperative of *aller* is **Va !** — the **s** is dropped. But before *y* the **s comes back**: **Vas-y !** Two vowels colliding is harder to say than one extra consonant, so French puts the **s** back purely for sound. With *vous* nothing changes: **Allez-y !**

steps.title: La maison de mes rêves
steps.body: The ideal home uses the **conditional**, which you already have from the ideal holiday. Here it joins the new material: *chez*, *y*, and the rooms. On the Pearson specification the conditional is Higher tier, apart from *je voudrais*.

visuals.problem: Say in French: *My ideal house would be by the sea. It would have six rooms and a big garden. I would live there with my family, and we could go to the beach on foot.*

steps.text: **Ma maison idéale serait au bord de la mer** — *serait* is the conditional of *être*
steps.note: the conditional stem of *être* is *ser-*: *je serais, ce serait*

steps.text: **Elle aurait six pièces** — *aurait* is the conditional of *avoir*
steps.note: and **pièces**, not *chambres*: six bedrooms would be a different claim

steps.text: **et un grand jardin** — *grand* goes **before** the noun
steps.note: *grand* is one of the short adjectives that precede

steps.text: **J'y habiterais avec ma famille** — **y** replaces *dans cette maison*
steps.note: before the verb, and *je* elides to *j'*

steps.text: **et on pourrait aller à la plage à pied** — *pourrait* is the conditional of *pouvoir*
steps.note: an infinitive follows a modal, as always

steps.text: Or, using *y* once more: *on pourrait **y** aller à pied*
steps.note: with an infinitive, *y* goes before the **infinitive**, not before *pourrait*

check.solution: **J'y vais.** *Y* replaces *à la piscine* and goes **before** the verb, and *je* elides to **j'**.

steps.title: Rêve et réalité
steps.body:
The best answers on this topic **contrast** the real home with the ideal one. That gives you two tenses, an opinion and a reason — and it is far easier than inventing a fantasy from nothing.

**The shape:**

1. **What is true now** — present: *J'habite dans un appartement en banlieue.*
2. **What you think of it** — opinion and reason: *C'est pratique parce que c'est près du collège, mais c'est un peu petit.*
3. **What you would prefer** — conditional: *Ma maison idéale serait plus grande, avec un jardin.*
4. **Why** — reason: *parce que j'aimerais avoir un chien.*

That is four sentences and it uses the present, an opinion, the conditional and a reason. Nothing in it is hard.

**Useful phrases for the contrast:**

- **par contre** — on the other hand
- **tandis que** — whereas
- **alors que** — whereas
- **en revanche** — on the other hand
- **ce qui me plaît, c'est…** — what I like is…
- **ce qui me manque, c'est…** — what I miss is…

**Ce qui me manque** is worth having exactly right. *Manquer* works backwards in French: the **thing** is the subject. *Un jardin me manque* — literally *a garden is lacking to me*, so **I miss a garden**. Get the subject the wrong way round and you have said the opposite.

steps.title: À toi : ta maison idéale
steps.body:
**Partie A.** Réécris avec *y* :

1. Je vais au cinéma.
2. Nous habitons dans cette maison.
3. Je suis allé en France.
4. On peut aller à la plage à pied.

**Partie B.** Complète avec *chez* ou *à* :

5. Je rentre ___ moi.
6. Je vais ___ la piscine.
7. On mange ___ mes grands-parents.
8. Elle est ___ la maison.

**Partie C.**

9. Décris ta maison en trois phrases : où elle est, combien de pièces, et où est ta chambre.
10. Écris quatre phrases sur ta maison idéale, en suivant la forme de l'étape 6 : la réalité, ton opinion, le rêve, et la raison.

For question 3, remember that *y* goes before the **auxiliary**, not before the participle.

steps.title: Aller plus loin
steps.body:
**Y before the infinitive, not the modal.** *Je vais **y** aller*, not *j'y vais aller*. This is the case that separates a rule from a habit. *Y* belongs to the verb that governs the place: in *je vais aller au marché*, it is **aller** that goes to the market, not *vais*. So *y* attaches to *aller*. The same logic puts it before the auxiliary in the perfect — *j'**y** suis allé* — because there the auxiliary and participle are one verb, and *y* goes at the front of it.

**Vas-y.** The *tu* imperative of an *-er* verb drops its **s**: *tu manges* → *Mange !*, *tu vas* → *Va !* But before *y* the **s** returns: **Vas-y !** Nothing grammatical has changed — it is purely for sound, because *va-y* puts two vowels together. French does the same in *Manges-en !* This is a small thing to know and it looks like real command of the language rather than of a textbook.

**Chez has no English word.** That is the point worth making in a writing task. English says *at Marie's* and leaves you to guess whether it is her house, her shop or her office; French says *chez Marie* and means *at Marie's place*, whatever that is. And *chez* does not change for movement: *je vais chez moi* and *je suis chez moi* use the same word, where English switches between *go home* and *at home*.

**Une chambre is a bedroom.** *Ma maison a six chambres* claims six **bedrooms** — a large house. *Six pièces* is what you meant. Examiners notice, because the two sentences describe different buildings.

**Les toilettes takes a plural verb.** *Les toilettes **sont** au rez-de-chaussée.* It is one of a small set of French nouns that are plural where English is singular, and the verb has to follow.

**Manquer runs backwards.** *Un jardin me manque* = *I miss a garden*. The thing missed is the **subject**. *Je manque un jardin* would mean you failed to catch or hit a garden, as in *je manque le bus*, I miss the bus. If you are not certain, use *j'aimerais avoir un jardin* instead — a mark for a conditional is worth more than a mark lost for a reversed verb.

**Contrast beats description.** Four sentences that set the real home against the ideal one give two tenses, two opinions and a link word. Eight sentences listing rooms give one tense and no opinions. The shorter answer scores higher.

steps.title: Résumé
steps.body:
- **J'habite dans une maison / un appartement**, **en ville**, **à la campagne**, **en banlieue**.
- Floors run as in Britain: **le rez-de-chaussée**, **le premier étage**, **le deuxième étage** — and take **au**.
- **Une chambre** is a **bedroom**; **une pièce** is any room.
- **Les toilettes** is plural: *les toilettes **sont**…*
- **Chez** means *at the home of* and takes a **person**: *chez moi*, *chez Marie*, *chez le médecin*.
- *Chez* does not change for movement: *je vais chez moi*, *je suis chez moi*.
- For a **place**, use *à*, *dans* or *en*: *à la maison*, *dans la cuisine*, *en ville*.
- **Y** means *there* and replaces a whole place phrase.
- **Y goes immediately before the verb it belongs to**: *j'y vais*, *nous y habitons*.
- Perfect tense: before the **auxiliary** — *j'y suis allé*.
- With an infinitive: before the **infinitive** — *je vais y aller*, *on peut y aller*.
- *Je* elides before *y*: **j'y**, never *je y*.
- Imperative: **Vas-y !** — the **s** returns for sound. **Allez-y !**
- The ideal home uses the **conditional**: *serait*, *aurait*, *j'habiterais*, *on pourrait*.
- Best answer shape: **reality, opinion, dream, reason** — four sentences, two tenses.
- **Manquer runs backwards**: *un jardin me manque* = *I miss a garden*.

questions.modelAnswer:
**Une réponse complète :**

*J'habite dans un appartement en banlieue, au troisième étage. Il y a **cinq pièces**. **J'y** habite depuis huit ans et **ce qui me plaît, c'est** que c'est près du collège, donc je peux **y** aller à pied. **Par contre**, c'est un peu petit. Ma maison idéale **serait** à la campagne et elle **aurait** un grand jardin, **parce que** j'aimerais avoir un chien.*

**Ce qui compte ici :**

- **Cinq pièces**, not *cinq chambres* — five bedrooms would describe a different flat.
- **J'y habite** — *y* before the verb, and *je* elided to *j'*.
- **Je peux y aller** — with an infinitive, *y* goes before the **infinitive**.
- **Serait** and **aurait** — the conditional carries the whole second half.
- **Par contre** marks the turn from reality to dream, which is what makes it an argument rather than a list.

**Pour aller plus loin :** *si j'avais le choix, j'habiterais près de la mer, mais je sais que ce n'est pas réaliste* adds *si* + imperfect + conditional, and a note of self-awareness that reads as a real opinion rather than an exercise.

questions.prompt: Explain where the pronoun *y* goes in a French sentence, and explain why it goes in a different place when there is an infinitive.
questions.solution: Le pronom y veut dire there et il remplace toute une expression qui nomme un lieu, par exemple à Paris, chez moi ou dans ma chambre. Il se place juste devant le verbe auquel il appartient, sauf à l'impératif affirmatif (vas-y). Dans un temps simple, c'est devant le verbe conjugué : je vais à Paris devient j'y vais. Au passé composé, il se place devant l'auxiliaire et non devant le participe passé : je suis allé en France devient j'y suis allé, parce que l'auxiliaire et le participe forment ensemble un seul verbe et que y se met au début de ce verbe. Mais quand il y a un infinitif, y se place devant l'infinitif : je vais aller au marché devient je vais y aller, et non j'y vais aller. La raison est logique : y appartient au verbe qui gouverne le lieu, et ici c'est aller qui va au marché, pas vais. Il faut aussi se rappeler que je devient j' devant y, parce que y commence par un son de voyelle. Enfin, à l'impératif, va reprend son s devant y, uniquement pour la prononciation : on dit vas-y et non va-y.

Covers the case with an infinitive
Explains the reason behind the infinitive case

questions.modelAnswer:
**Ce que *y* remplace.** A whole phrase naming a **place**: *à Paris*, *chez moi*, *dans ma chambre*, *en France*.

**La règle.** *Y* goes **immediately before the verb it belongs to**.

- Simple tense: **j'y vais**, **nous y habitons**
- Perfect: before the **auxiliary** — **j'y suis allé**, because the auxiliary and participle are one verb and *y* goes at its front
- With an infinitive: before the **infinitive** — **je vais y aller**, not *j'y vais aller*

**Pourquoi l'infinitif est différent.** *Y* attaches to the verb that **governs the place**. In *je vais aller au marché*, it is **aller** that goes to the market — *vais* only says when. So *y* goes with *aller*.

**Deux détails.** *Je* elides to **j'** before *y*. And in the imperative the **s** returns for sound only: **Vas-y !**, **Allez-y !**

questions.prompt: Complete with the conditional of *avoir*: *Ma maison idéale ______ un grand jardin.* (would have)
questions.solution: **aurait**. The conditional is the future stem **aur-** plus the imperfect ending **-ait**: *elle aurait*, *il y aurait*.

examTechnique.body:
Put y immediately before the verb it belongs to, which is the infinitive whenever there is one.

In the perfect tense, put y before the auxiliary and not before the participle.

Elide je to j' before y.

Use chez with a person and à, dans or en with a place.

Say pièces for rooms in general and chambres only for bedrooms.

Give les toilettes a plural verb.

Structure a written answer as reality, opinion, dream, reason, so that it carries two tenses.

If you are unsure of manquer, write j'aimerais avoir instead: a conditional is worth more than a reversed verb.
examinerErrors: Writing je y vais instead of j'y vais.
Writing j'y vais aller instead of je vais y aller.
Putting y before the participle rather than the auxiliary, as in je suis y allé.
Using chez with a place, as in chez la maison.
Writing six chambres when six pièces is meant.
Giving les toilettes a singular verb.
Reversing manquer, so that I miss a garden becomes something else.
Listing rooms at length instead of contrasting the real home with the ideal one.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer places *y* without hesitating, because it knows *y* attaches to the verb that governs the place — which settles *je vais y aller* and *j'y suis allé* with the same thought. It uses *chez* naturally and knows it covers both going and being. It says *pièces* when it means rooms. And rather than describing a house at length, it sets the real home against the ideal one in four sentences, which carries two tenses, two opinions and a reason, and reads like a person talking rather than a vocabulary list.
